rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading takes ʿāṣim literally and man raḥima as the one shown mercy: none protects from God’s decree, but one whom He pities is protected; the exception is disconnected.
rows.anchor: والثالث أن عاصما على ظاهره و ( من رحم ) بمعنى المرحوم والإستثناء منقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This disconnected exception is challenged as uncommon because its clause differs from the first in both affirmation and nominal versus verbal form.
rows.anchor: مثل هذا المنقطع قليل لأنه في الحقيقة جملة منقطعة تخالف الأولى لا في النفي والإثبات فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth reading makes ʿāṣim mean maʿṣūm and man raḥima mean the merciful; the disconnected exception means only the merciful can rescue whomever he wills.
rows.anchor: والرابع أن عاصما بمعنى معصوم كدافق بمعنى مدفوق وفاتن بمعنى مفتون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited line uses fātin for one overcome, supporting ʿāṣim as the one protected.
rows.anchor: بطيء القيام رخيم الكلا م أمسى فؤادي به ( فاتنا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fifth reading supplies an omitted place and connects the exception: only the ark, place of the people shown mercy, protects; it fits the mountain refuge and ranks after the first reading.
rows.anchor: وهو وجه حسن فيه مقابلة لقوله : ( يعصمني )

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: The sixth reading means no protected one exists except the place of those shown mercy; by metonymy, protecting the ship protects its occupants.
rows.anchor: والسادس ما أبداه صاحب الكشف عنده وهو أن المعنى لا معصوم إلا مكان من رحمه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A seventh reading treats the exception as free: no person or place is protected except one whom God shows mercy.
rows.anchor: والسابع أن الاستثناء مفرغ والمعنى لا عاصم اليوم أحدا أو لأحد إلا من رحمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some call the free-exception reading closest, al-Ālūsī chooses none over the first interpretation.
rows.anchor: وعده بعضهم أقربها ولا أظنك تعدل بالوجه الأول وجها وهو الذي اختاره

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says lā’s predicate is omitted as understood, ‘existent’; Hijazi speakers commonly omit it, while Tamim speakers require it.
rows.anchor: والظاهر على ما قال أبو حيان : أن خبر لا محذوف للعلم به أي ( لا عاصم ) موجود

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: He makes al-yawm accusative through an implied verb indicated by ʿāṣim, with min amr Allāh attached to that verb.
rows.anchor: ويكون اليوم منصوبا على إضماره فعل يدل عليه ( عاصم ) أي ( لا عاصم ) يعصم اليوم

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥūfī allows al-yawm and the prepositional phrase to attach to an omitted predicate, or al-yawm to modify ʿāṣim with that phrase as predicate.
rows.anchor: وجوز الحوفي أن يكون ( اليوم ) متعلقا بمحذوف وقع خبرا للا والجار متعلق بذلك المحذوف أيضا

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ rejects a time adverb as predicate of a concrete noun; he makes min amr Allāh govern the noun and the prepositional phrase the predicate. Abū Ḥayyān also rejects the adverb as modifier.
rows.anchor: ورد أبو البقاء خبرية اليوم بأنه ظرف زمان وهو لا يكون خبرا عن الجثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wave cut off Noah’s exchange with his son; a report says a huge wave arrived before their conversation ended and swallowed the son and his horse, while he rode proudly.
rows.anchor: فإنقطع ما بينهما من المجاوبة قيل : كانا يتراجعان الكلام فما إستتمت المراجعة حتى جاءت موجة عظيمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse itself only states that the wave intervened; Noah learned of his son’s drowning afterward.
rows.anchor: وليس في الآية هنا إلا إثبات الحيلولة وأما علمه عليه السلام بغرقه فلم يحصل إلا بعد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reads ‘between them’ as between Noah’s son and the mountain; Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh transmit it from al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazza.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : بينهما أي بين ابن نوح عليه السلام والجبل وأخرج ذلك ابن أبي حاتم وأبو الشيخ

rows.speaker: أبو السعود
rows.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd objects that the son’s drowning follows the wave separating him from Noah, since the mountain could not protect him even without a wave between him and the refuge.
rows.anchor: إنما يتفرع على حيلولة الموج بينه عليه السلام وبين ابنه لا بينه وبين الجبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reply says the consequence need not be immediate, or that the son assumed the water would not reach him.
rows.anchor: وأجيب بأن التفريع لا ينافي ذلك لأن المراد فكان من غير مهلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse depicts unbelievers’ drowning as emphatically certain; kāna intensifies their being among the drowned rather than merely becoming so.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دلالة على غرق سأ الكفرة على أبلغ وجه فكأن ذلك أمر مقرر الوقوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After explaining disputes over monotheism and prophethood and promises and threats, God commands the Messenger to remain steadfast as commanded, implying another revelation, perhaps non-recited.
rows.anchor: لما بين أمر المختلفين في التوحيد والنبوة وأطنب سبحانه في شرح الوعد والوعيد أمر رسوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uprightness is lasting adherence to the balanced path between excess and deficiency, comprehensive of knowledge, action, character, beliefs, shared duties, and the Prophet’s special mission.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن هذا أمر بالدوام على الإستقامة وهي لزوم المنهج المستقيم وهو المتوسط بين الإفراط والتفريط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Perfect balance requires total dependence on God; it is likened to a line between sun and shade, and its difficulty is illustrated by 17:74. It requires spiritual support and clinging to truth.
rows.anchor: لا يحصل إلا بالإفتقار إلى الله تعالى ونفي الحول والقوة بالكلية ومثلوا الأمر المتوسط بين ذينك الطرفين بخط يكون بين الشمس والظل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reports that after this verse descended, the Prophet said ‘Be earnest, be earnest,’ and was not seen laughing afterward; Ibn ʿAbbās called it the hardest verse to bear.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن أنه قال : لما نزلت هذه الآية قال صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم : شمروا شمروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some cite ‘Hūd made me gray’ as proof of hardship, but reports add other sūrahs too; al-Kashf says singling out Hūd is not evident because its sister sūrahs do not mention uprightness.
rows.anchor: من قوله صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم : شيبتني هود

rows.speaker: ابن عساكر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAsākir transmits from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, from his father, the Prophet’s statement that Hūd, its sister sūrahs, and what befell earlier nations made him gray.
rows.anchor: ما أخرجه ابن عساكر عن جعفر بن محمد

rows.speaker: الشهاب
rows.claim: Al-Shihāb explains Hūd’s special effect by its structure: it guides the Prophet through the methods and hardships of calling people from beginning to end, rather than merely consoling him.
rows.anchor: مبنى هذه السورة الكريمة على إرشاده تعالى شأنه نبيه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم إلى كيفية الدعوة

rows.speaker: الشهاب
rows.claim: This concluding verse summarizes the sūrah; its burdens made the Prophet fear accountability for failing them. Other sūrahs’ Judgment scenes recalled Hūd’s guidance, without implying any conflict with infallibility.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت هذه السورة جامعة لإرشاده من أول أمره إلى آخرخ وهذه الآية فذلكة لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report continues that Hūd and its sister sūrahs and what earlier nations suffered made the Prophet gray; this does not conflict with reports naming Hūd alone or this verse.
rows.anchor: قال : شيبتني هود وأخواتها وما فعل بالأمم قبلي

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others take kāf in kamā as ‘upon,’ meaning remain upon the Qurʾān; Muqātil says remain upon monotheism, and Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says report truthfully about God with firm resolve.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية وجماعة : المعنى إستقم على القرآن وقال مقاتل : إمض على التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the broad sense: remain upright in everything God commanded.
rows.anchor: والأظهر إبقاء ما على العموم أي إستقم على جميع ما أمرت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account keeps kāf comparative but treats it like mathal in ‘one like you is not miserly’; al-Ālūsī says comparing a thing with itself is unnecessary. Abū Ḥayyān supplies ‘the like of what the command seeks.’
rows.anchor: إنها في حكم مثل في قولهم : مثلك لا يبخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A more remote reading makes kāf mean ‘upon’ and istifʿāl a request, yielding ‘seek establishment upon the religion.’
rows.anchor: وأبعد بعضهم فجعل الكاف بمعنى على واستفعل للطلب كاستغفر الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who repented with the Prophet abandoned associating partners and believed with him; their companionship may refer to shared repentance without specifying its object.
rows.anchor: ومن تاب معك ( أي تاب من الشرك وآمن معك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet used to seek God’s forgiveness more than seventy times daily.
rows.anchor: يستغفر الله تعالى في اليوم أكثر من سبعين مرة

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān and others coordinate man with the implicit subject of ‘be steadfast’; others prefer an omitted verb because an imperative does not take an overt subject.
rows.anchor: و ( من ) على ما اختاره أبو حيان وجماعة عطف على الضمير المستكن في ( واستقم )

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ allows a comitative object: be steadfast alongside those who repented; a nominal clause with an omitted predicate is another view.
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو البقاء كونه منصوبا على أنه مفعول معه والمعنى استقم مصاحبا لمن تاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Do not exceed bounds by excess or deficiency; Ibn ʿAbbās says not to declare Qurʾānic lawful and unlawful without command, Ibn Zayd says do not disobey God, and Muqātil says do not mix monotheism with idolatry; the broad sense is preferred.
rows.anchor: ولا تطغوا ( أي لا تنحرفوا عما حد لكم بإفراط أو تفريط فإن كلا طرفي قصد الأمور ذميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God sees and recompenses people’s acts; this explains the preceding command and prohibition. Some read the verb in the third person.
rows.anchor: فيجازيكم على ذلك وهو تعليل للأمر والنهي السابقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some infer that explicit texts must be followed without bending them to desire or unaided reason; analogy grounded in textual causes counts as following authorized ijtihād. The Imam objects to specifying general texts by analogy.
rows.anchor: دليل على وجوب إتباع المنصوص عليه من غير إنحراف بمجرد التشهي وإعمال العقل الصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the Imam’s proof that ablution limbs must follow Qurʾānic word order: the same logic would order every pair of commands joined by wa, such as prayer and alms, which is untenable.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن إيجاب الترتيب في الوضوء لذلك ليس بشيء ويلزمه أن يوجب الترتيب في الأوامر المتعاطفة بالواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument unjustly implies that Ḥanafīs who do not require ablution order are tyrants outside God’s bounds, with no possibility of being upright.
rows.anchor: يجزم بأن الحنفية الذين لا يوجبون الترتيب في أعمال الوضوء طاغون خارجون عما حد الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Establish the prescribed prayers fully; other reported meanings are to maintain them regularly or perform them at the start of their times.
rows.anchor: أي المكتوبة ومعنى إقامتها أداؤها على تمامها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two ends mean the beginning and end of the day. Zulf are hours near the day; al-Layth and Thaʿlab say the first part of night, while Abū ʿUbayda, al-Akhfash, and Ibn Qutayba say any night hour, supported by al-ʿAjjāj’s verse.
rows.anchor: فإنه من أزلفه إذا قربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zulf is coordinated with the two ends, and min al-layl qualifies it. End prayers are variously dawn and afternoon, dawn and sunset, or dawn then noon and afternoon; Abū Ḥayyān favors dawn and afternoon, while noon as an endpoint is questioned.
rows.anchor: وهو عطف على ( طرفي النهار ) و ( من الليل ) في موضع الصفة له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most identify the night prayers as sunset and evening; a report via al-Ḥasan from Ibn ʿAbbās specifies ʿatama. Another reading makes zulf night prayers drawing near to God, perhaps the Prophet’s night prayer or evening and witr.
rows.anchor: والمراد بصلاة الزلف عند الأكثر صلاة المغرب والعشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭalḥa, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and Abū Jaʿfar read zuluf with a rounded lām; Mujāhid and Ibn Muḥayṣin read it with a silent lām, and a variant has zulfa, a synonymous form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة وابن أبي إسحاق وأبو جعفر ( زلفا ) بضم اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good deeds expiate sins and remove liability, not sins as entities; another view says their records are erased. The view that they prevent sinning is remote and contrary to reports.
rows.anchor: أي يكفرنها ويذهبن المؤاخذة عليها وإلا فنفس السيئات أعراض وجدت فانعدمت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent scope is obligatory and voluntary good deeds, though some restrict it to obligations. Reports about affirmation matching angels, fasting ʿArafa, and gratitude after eating or dressing support voluntary acts as expiators.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد من الحسنات ما يعم الصلوات المفروضة وغيرها من الطاعات

rows.speaker: أبو اليسر
rows.claim: The occasion is reported as Abū al-Yusr regretting he kissed a woman; after waiting for revelation, the Prophet said prayer atoned for it. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and Ibn al-Musayyib also transmit this view.
rows.anchor: أبا اليسر من الأنصار قبل امرأة ثم ندم فأتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who identify good deeds as obligatory prayers likely cite one important instance in the general category; the occasion does not restrict the verse.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن ذلك منهم إقتصار على بعض مهم من أفراد ذلك العام وسبب النزول لا يأبى العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most take ‘sins’ as minor sins and say major sins require repentance, citing Muslim’s report through al-ʿAlāʾ that five prayers expiate the interval if major sins are avoided.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالسيآت عند الأكثرين الصغائر لأن الكبائر لا يكفرها

rows.speaker: البلقيني
rows.claim: Al-Balqīnī says 4:31 concerns avoiding major sins throughout life, whereas the prayer report concerns each day; al-Samhūdī objects that lifelong avoidance entails daily prayer, then discusses multiple expiators retaining their rewards.
rows.anchor: وأجاب البلقيني بأن ذلك غير وارد لأن المراد بالآية أن تجتنبوا في جميع العمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects a lifelong reading of 4:31: the reward for avoiding major sins at each time expiates minor sins committed then, as al-Qāḍī and al-Ghazālī support.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد من ذلك أن ثواب إجتناب الكبائر في كل وقت يكفر الصغائر

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: Al-Ghazālī says restraint expiates only when someone has ability and desire to commit a major sin; abstaining from incapacity or lack of desire does not earn that effect.
rows.anchor: إجتناب الكبيرة إنما يكفر الصغيرة إذا إجتنبها مع القدرة والإرادة

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Al-Nawawī says that when an expiatory act coincides with major sins but no minor sins, one may hope that the major sins are lightened.
rows.anchor: أنه صادف فعل المكفر كبيرة أو كبائر ولم يصادف صغيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī reconciles the evidence by making avoidance of major sins a limit on expiating all interval sins, not a condition for any expiation: prayers expiate minors and all interval sins when majors are avoided.
rows.anchor: ما اجتنبت الكبائر في الخبر ليس قيدا لأصل التكفير بل لشمول التكفير سائر الذنوب التي بين الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: ابن حجر
rows.claim: Ibn Ḥajar says avoiding major sins entails performing the five prayers, since abandoning prayer is major; al-Ālūsī says this argument merits examination.
rows.anchor: وعلى تقدير ورد السؤال فالتخلص عنه سهل وذلك لأنه لا يتم إجتناب الكبائر إلا بفعل الصلوات الخمس

rows.speaker: المحب الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Muḥibb al-Ṭabarī records two views: the majority make avoidance of major sins a condition; another treats it as an exception, so expiation excludes major sins, which he calls stronger.
rows.anchor: إختلف العلماء في أمر تكفير الصغائر بالعبادات هل هو مشروط بإجتناب الكبائر على قولين

rows.speaker: الزركشي
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashī reports disagreement over requiring repentance for expiation; al-Baḥr says the requirement is explicit among rigorous legal theorists.
rows.anchor: ذكر الزركشي أنهم إختلفوا في أن التكفير هل يشترط فيه التوبة أم لا

rows.speaker: السبكي
rows.claim: Al-Subkī says acceptance of repentance from unbelief is certain by grace, but acceptance for sins is disputed; other authorities differ over whether its expiation is presumptive or certain.
rows.anchor: والمنقول عن السبكي أنه قال : إن قبول التوبة عن الكفر مقطوع به تفضلا

rows.speaker: أهل السنة
rows.claim: Al-Nasafī, Ṣadr al-Sharīʿa, and other Sunni scholars allow punishment for minor sins even when major sins are avoided, citing 4:48 and 18:49; the Muʿtazila deny it based on 4:31, which may concern unbelief.
rows.anchor: أن العقاب على الصغائر جائز الوقوع سواء إجتنب مرتكبها الكبائر أم لا

rows.speaker: صاحب الذخائر
rows.claim: The author of al-Dhakhāʾir argues that some good deeds expiate minor and major sins, citing reports promising forgiveness of past and future sins; Ibn al-Mundhir leans this way.
rows.anchor: وذهب صاحب الذخائر إلى أن من الحسنات ما يكفر الصغائر والكبائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Critics call broad expiation ignorance and agreement with the Murjiʾa, arguing repentance would be pointless; al-Ālūsī replies that expiation differs from Murjiʾism and repentance remains obligatory for new and recurring delay sins.
rows.anchor: إن الكبائر والصغائر تكفرها الطهارة والصلاة لظاهر الأحاديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past expiation does not remove the ongoing duty to repent, just as a sleeper whose prayer time passed must still make it up; the Abū Hurayra report is specific and cannot be extended by analogy.
rows.anchor: ولا يلزم من تكفير الله تعالى ذنوب عبده سقوط التكليف بالتوبة التي كلف بها تكليفا مستمرا

rows.speaker: الأشعري
rows.claim: Repentance for minor sins is obligatory according to al-Ashʿarī, with al-Juwaynī and al-Anṣārī reporting consensus; ʿIzz al-Dīn ibn ʿAbd al-Salām says delay incurs renewed sin over time.
rows.anchor: التوبة من الصغائر واجبة على ما نقل عن الأشعري وحكى إمام الحرمين وتلميذه الأنصاري الإجماع عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder benefits those who heed admonition, singled out because they are the ones who benefit.
rows.anchor: أي عظة للمتعظين وخصهم بالذكر لأنهم المنتفعون بها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says ‘that’ refers to the counsel about uprightness, avoiding tyranny and inclination toward wrongdoers, and establishing prayer at the named times; Abū Ḥayyān prefers prayer alone.
rows.anchor: والإشارة إلى ما تقدم من الوصية بالإستقامة والنهي عن الطغيان والركون إلى الذين ظلموا

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī takes the reference as the sūrah’s commands and prohibitions; others identify the Qurʾān, or prayer and repentance.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى الأوامر والنواهي في هذه السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Be patient through the hardships of fulfilling what you have been charged to do. Al-Kashshāf says the renewed command highlights patience’s special merit and necessity for obedience and avoiding prohibitions.
rows.anchor: أي على مشاق إمتثال ما كلفت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uprightness entails perseverance in speech, action, and belief, hence patience in obedience and avoiding disobedience; another view makes patience continual, like the prayer command in 20:132.
rows.anchor: بأن الأمر بالإستقامة أمر بالثبات قولا وفعلا وعقدا وهو الصبر على طاعة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A defense says resisting natural inclination toward tyranny or wrongdoers is difficult; al-Ālūsī replies that natural side effects are not prohibited, as loving one’s unbelieving child is not sinful, and the total burden of duties suffices.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن ما هو من توابع الطبيعة لا يكون من متعلقات النهي ولهذا ذكروا أن حب المسلم لولده الكافر مثلا لا إثم فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God fully pays those who do good without loss, proving His freedom from depriving them and grounding patience; this patience is ihsān. Muqātil says ihsān is sincerity, Ibn ʿAbbās says those who pray.
rows.anchor: أي يوفيهم ثواب أعمالهم من غير بخس أصلا وعبر عن ذلك بنفي الإضاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commands to do good are singularly addressed to the Prophet though general in meaning, while prohibitions use the plural for the community, honoring him.
rows.anchor: ومن البلاغة القرآنية أن الأوامر بأفعال الخير أفردت للنبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph answers an implied question by privately appealing to God. Al-sijn normally means prison; several readers pronounce it with fatḥa as the verbal noun ‘imprisoning.’
rows.anchor: بياني كأن سائلا يقول : فماذا صنع يوسف حينئذ

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: ʿUthmān, Ṭāriq, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Zuhrī, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ibn Hurmuz, and Yaʿqūb read al-sajn with fatḥa as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عثمان ومولاه طارق وزيد بن علي والزهري وابن أبي إسحاق وابن هرمز ويعقوب ( السجن ) بفتح السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph says prison is preferable because brief hardship leads to lasting relief; the alternative is compliance with the women and painful punishment. The comparative is not literal since he has no desire for their request.
rows.anchor: آثر عندي لأن فيه مشقة قليلة نافدة إثرها راحات كثيرة أبدية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling prison ‘beloved’ cuts off their hope that fear will make him cooperate; reports say the women threatened him and individually sought him in private.
rows.anchor: وصيغة التفضيل ليست على بابها إذ ليس له عليه السلام شائبة محبة لما يدعونه إليه

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn reports that each woman secretly sent Joseph a request to visit.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن الحسين رضي الله تعالى عنهما أن كل واحدة منهن أرسلت إليه سرا تسأله الزيارة

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī cites a report that God told Joseph prison was his own doing because he asked for it instead of safety; al-Tirmidhī transmits the Prophet’s advice to ask for well-being rather than patience in affliction from Muʿādh ibn Jabal.
rows.anchor: وفي أثر ذكره القرطبي أنه عليه السلام لما قال : ( رب السجن أحب إلي )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph asks God to deflect the women’s plot by sustaining his chastity; he attributes good and escape from evil to divine favor rather than his own power.
rows.anchor: في تحبيب ذلك إلي وتحسينه لدي بأن تثبتني على ما أنا عليه من العصمة والعفة

rows.speaker: أبو السعود
rows.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd says Joseph admits a natural impulse and pleads like a desperate person: save me or I perish. Al-Qutb and others call this a Muʿtazilī evasion of the Ashʿarī inference that God turns the servant from sin.
rows.anchor: لا أنه عليه السلام يطلب الإجبار الإلجاء إلى العصمة والعفة وفي نفسه داعية تدعوه إلى السوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Illā contracts from in lā, the conditional particle plus negation, with n assimilated into lām; aṣbu is jussive as apodosis, from ṣabā, to incline toward desire.
rows.anchor: وأصل ( إلا ) إن لا فهي مركبة من إن الشرطية ولا النافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional clause coordinates with ‘prison is dearer’; the nominal first clause expresses an enduring preference. Another reading derives aṣbu from intense yearning that flows toward its object.
rows.anchor: وجيء بالأولى إسمية دون الثانية لأن أحبيته السجن مما يدعونه إليه كانت ثابتة مستمرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Among the ignorant’ means those who do not act on knowledge or fools who commit ugly acts; the poetic line uses ignorance to mean folly rather than lack of knowledge.
rows.anchor: أي الذين لا يعملون بما يعلمون لأن من لا جدوى لعلمه فهو ومن لا يعلم سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God answered the plea implied by ‘unless You turn away their plot’; the implied request is even stronger than an explicit request to turn it away.
rows.anchor: فاستجاب له ربه ( أي أجاب له على أبلغ وجه دعاءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God Joseph’s Lord and beginning the prayer with that address express tenderness; God deflected the plot by sustaining chastity and keeping him from sin.
rows.anchor: وفي إسناد الإستجابة إلى الرب مضافا إلى ضميره عليه السلام ما لا يخفى من إظهار اللطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God hears the distressed person’s supplication and knows their state, intentions, and what benefits them.
rows.anchor: السميع ( لدعاء المتضرعين إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs proving Joseph’s innocence include the torn shirt and women cutting their hands; Qatāda limits the signs to the shirt tear, treating the dual as plural. Mujāhid counts only the tear, since the cuts do not prove innocence.
rows.anchor: وطهارته من قد القميص وقطع النساء أيديهن وعليهما إقتصر قتادة فيما أخرجه عنه ابن جرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the women’s cuts show Joseph’s beauty made them the likely initiators; others count his refusal of them as evidence of innocence because the ruler and advisers heard it. Ikrima reports Ibn ʿAbbās also named marks on Joseph’s body and a knife mark.
rows.anchor: وجه بعضهم عد القطع من الشواهد بأن حسنه عليه الصلاة والسلام الفاتن للنساء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ikrima asked Ibn ʿAbbās about the signs; he listed the shirt tear, marks on Joseph’s body, and a knife mark. Other signs may have been omitted, as prophetic miracles often are.
rows.anchor: سألت ابن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما عن الآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The subject of badā may be the verbal noun ‘decision,’ an opinion, or imprisonment understood from ‘they will imprison him’; the oath and response may be an object of implied saying or an explanatory clause.
rows.anchor: وفاعل ( بدا ) ضمير يعود إما للبداء مصدر الفعل المذكور أو بمعنى الرأي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes ‘they will surely imprison him’ the response to badā; another makes the full proposition its subject, as in 36:31 and 14:45, though most grammarians reject this.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إن جملة ( ليسجننه ) جواب لبدا لأنه من أفعال القلوب

rows.speaker: المازني
rows.claim: Al-Māzinī selects the first subject analysis; Abū Ḥayyān selects the final one, where a pronoun refers to imprisonment understood from the sentence.
rows.anchor: واختار المازني في الفاعل الوجه الأول

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān selects the final analysis of the subject of badā.
rows.anchor: واختار أبو حيان الوجه الأخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The decision to imprison Joseph arose when his wife persuaded her husband, who yielded to her and entrusted his authority to her; a report says she framed Joseph as the offender and demanded his imprisonment.
rows.anchor: وكان ذلك البداء بإستنزال المرأة لزوجها ومطاوعته لها وحبه إياها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan reads latasjunannahu as a direct address to the ruler or the ruler and advisers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن لتسجننه على صيغة الخطاب بأن خاطب بعضهم العزيز ومن يليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says ‘until a time’ means until city talk and rumors die down; the ruler’s apparent aim was temporary, while the wife wanted prison to humiliate Joseph and make people think him guilty.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : إلى إنقطاع المقال وما شاع في المدينة من الفاحشة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports give five, seven, or twelve years; al-Ālūsī avoids fixing a number and says only that the imprisonment was long. For most, ḥīn is an indefinite period, short or long.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل : إنه عليه السلام حبس إثنتي عشرة سنة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd reportedly read ʿattā with ʿayn, a Hudhayl dialect; ʿUmar wrote directing him to recite Quraysh’s ḥattā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود عتى بإبدال حاء ( حتى ) عينا وهي لغة هذيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two young men were servants of the greater king Rayyān ibn al-Walīd: one baker and one cupbearer; an account says they were jailed after a poisoning plot against the king.
rows.anchor: غلامان كانا للملك الأكبر الريان بن الوليد : أحدهما خبازه وصاحب طعامه والآخر ساقيه

rows.speaker: ابن إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Isḥāq says the two loved Joseph when they saw him; Joseph begged them not to, since everyone who loved him suffered a trial, but they persisted.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج غير واحد عن ابن إسحق أنهما لما رأياه قالا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling their imprisonment ‘entering with him’ may suggest it became easier on seeing Joseph; another view says the wording associates Joseph with their prison status and avoids wording that denies his choice. Maʿa ordinarily implies concurrence from the action’s beginning.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن مع تدل على الصحبة والمقارنة لفاعل الفعل في ابتداء تلبسه بالفعل

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: For the Queen’s ‘I submitted with Solomon,’ al-Kashf allows ‘with’ to mean submission to God and the Messenger, rather than simultaneous companionship; it suggests she had considered herself religious before her new Islam followed the Prophet’s guidance.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب الكشف : إنه لا يتعين المحكي عنها المعية الفاعل فجاز أن يراد أسلمت لله ولرسوله مثلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some distinguish ongoing Islam from punctual entry, but al-Ālūsī prefers concurrence as the original meaning whenever possible. The object precedes the subject for emphasis; ‘with him’ precedes prison because companionship matters more.
rows.anchor: واختير أن المقارنة هي الأصل ولا يعدل عنها ما أمكنت فتأمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sentence follows an implied ‘they imprisoned him’; the two men entered with him. Al-sijn with fatḥa means the prison location, and ‘he said’ answers an implied question.
rows.anchor: كأنه قيل : فلما بدا لهم ذلك سجنوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cupbearer’s present-tense dream means he saw himself pressing wine, reportedly from a beautiful vine with three branches; grapes are named for the intended end product. Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd’s ‘grapes’ is gloss, not canonical recitation.
rows.anchor: وروي أنه قال : رأيت حبلة من كرم حسنة لها ثلاثة أغصان فيها عناقيد عنب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows ‘wine’ to be described as pressed because pressing is done for its sake; the common explanation is metonymy for its outcome. Al-Sijistānī heard reliable eloquent speakers use khamr as masculine.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية : يجوز أن يكون وصف الخمر بأنها معصورة لأن العصر من أجلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aranī lets subject and object pronouns identify the same person as with verbs of perception: ‘I saw myself pressing wine.’ The baker’s dream has bread, or tharīd in Ibn Masʿūd’s muṣḥaf as a gloss, with birds eating from the upper basket.
rows.anchor: وحاصله أرى نفسي أعصر خمرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Tell us its interpretation’ refers to both visions or what was seen; plural speech can narrate separate requests, as in 23:51. They call Joseph a benefactor for interpreting dreams or for his learning.
rows.anchor: أي أخبرنا بتأويله بتعبيره وما يؤول إليه أمره

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda reports that prison inmates were despondent; Joseph urged them to hope and be patient, and they praised his comfort. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says he tended the sick, made room for them, and gathered supplies for the needy.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن أبي حاتم وغيره عن قتادة قال : لما انتهى يوسف إلى السجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After proving his knowledge, Joseph resumes the answer with a repeated address because interpretation is a new topic; he means the cupbearer without naming him, trusting the interpretation and observing good companionship.
rows.anchor: بعد تحقيق الحق وبيانه لهما مقدار علمه الواسع شرع في إنبائهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph interprets the cupbearer’s vine as the king and restored favor; three branches mean three days until release and return to service. The baker’s three baskets mean three days until release and crucifixion, with birds eating his head.
rows.anchor: روي أنه عليه السلام قال له : ما رأيت من الكرمة وحسنها هو الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading has yusqā passive; another uses active asqā. Saqā and asqā can both mean giving drink, though convention distinguishes giving a drink from providing watering; ʿIkrima is also reported to read passively with riyyihi as second object.
rows.anchor: وقريء ( فيسقى ) بضم الياء والبناء للفاعل من أسقى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quḍiya means completed or settled: the matter the two men asked about has been decided.
rows.anchor: قضي ( أتم وأحكم ( الأمر الذي فيه تستفتيان
